job.title: Assistant Sales Manager - Full Time
job.company: AM Retail Group - Karl Lagerfeld Paris

realStack: Point-of-sale (POS) terminal and daily sales/transaction reporting
Visual merchandising standards and floor-set / planogram guides
Personal and store sales-goal tracking (KPIs: conversion, UPT, ADS, sales-per-hour)
Associate scheduling / floor-coverage planning and labor management
New-hire onboarding, training checklists and company-standard operating procedures
Coaching, performance-monitoring and recognition routines for sales associates
Customer-service protocols and clienteling / customer-relations practices
Brand portfolio context (Karl Lagerfeld Paris under AM Retail Group: Wilsons Leather, G.H. Bass, DKNY, Calvin Klein Performance)
coreResponsibilities: Hit personal sales goals while motivating the team to drive overall store sales performance
Deliver and model exemplary customer service, maximizing profitability through the customer experience
Maintain store presentation — clean, well-organized, and compliant with visual-merchandising standards
Direct associates on the floor to ensure coverage and completion of daily tasks
Train and orient new associates to company standards and develop a sales-focused staff
Monitor associate performance, coach to company expectations, and recognize successes to build morale
Act as second-in-command, partnering with the Store Manager on day-to-day operational effectiveness
statedVsRealGaps: seniorityTarget is set to 'senior', but the JD's actual bar — two years of specialty-retail leadership experience and only 'encouraged' post-secondary education — describes an early-to-mid-level floor leader, not a senior manager; this is the sharpest stated-vs-real divergence

The JD frames the role around driving 'business success' and 'operational effectiveness' yet never names the hard operational levers a real ASM owns — inventory/shrink control, loss prevention, cash handling, opening/closing, scheduling to labor budget; the work is implied but invisible in the stated need

Heavy weighting toward sales + service + associate coaching, near-silent on metrics ownership; a candidate reading the JD would underestimate the back-of-house and compliance load that the job actually carries

'Competitive salary and excellent benefits' is asserted with no band or structure, so the stated value exchange can't be evaluated against the real demands of a fast-paced, customer-first floor leadership role
riskAreas: Title/seniority inflation: recruiting a 'senior' candidate against a 2-year requirement risks either over-paying for floor work or attracting candidates who are surprised by the hands-on, task-level scope
Outcome depends heavily on the Store Manager partnership the JD names — a weak or absent SM relationship leaves the ASM owning the floor without the stated support structure
Specialty/fashion retail is a high-turnover environment; the 'train new associates' duty is likely continuous churn management, not occasional onboarding
Unstated operational accountability (shrink, scheduling, P&L contribution) means real performance will be judged on factors the JD never makes explicit — a fairness and expectation-setting risk
Physical, fast-paced, on-floor demands and standard retail hours (nights/weekends/holidays) are implied by the format but not disclosed, a common source of early attrition
analysis.reflection: Read against the real body of work a retail floor leader acts on, this is a well-defined, standardized assistant-manager role at a mid-market fashion banner — its true 'materials' are the POS, the floor-set, the sales KPIs, the schedule, and the associate roster, not a tech stack, and judged in those terms its complexity is solidly medium: people leadership plus sales plus implied store operations, all inside a large retailer's playbook. The need as stated is coherent on the sales-and-service axis but diverges from the evidence in two ways: it labels the role 'senior' while the qualifications describe an early-to-mid leader, and it foregrounds inspiration and customer experience while leaving the operational spine of the job (inventory, loss prevention, labor/scheduling, opening-closing) unstated. Hire for a strong floor-level sales coach who can run a shift and develop staff — not for a senior operator — and set expectations up front about the back-of-house accountability the JD omits.

role.title: Assistant Sales Manager
mustHaves: 2+ years of specialty retail experience in a leadership role (fashion/apparel retail strongly preferred)
Demonstrated ability to hit personal sales goals AND lift team/store sales performance, with fluency in core retail KPIs (conversion, UPT, ADS, sales-per-hour)
Exemplary, role-model-level customer service and clienteling; able to set the service standard others follow on the floor
Hands-on visual merchandising execution — floor sets, planogram/merchandising-standard compliance, and disciplined store presentation (clean, organized, on-brand)
People leadership on a fast-paced floor: directing associates, assigning floor coverage, and driving completion of daily tasks
Associate development — onboarding/training new hires to company SOPs, monitoring performance, and coaching to expectations
Strong interpersonal and verbal communication skills that translate directly into sales and customer relations
Ability to operate calmly and decisively in a high-traffic, fast-paced store environment
niceToHaves: Post-secondary education; a retail-management degree or coursework
Fluency with POS systems and daily sales/transaction reporting
Back-of-house operational ownership the JD implies but never states: inventory/shrink control, loss prevention, cash handling, and opening/closing procedures
Scheduling and labor-management experience (building coverage to a labor budget)
Experience within a multi-brand fashion portfolio (e.g., AM Retail Group brands: Wilsons Leather, G.H. Bass, DKNY, Calvin Klein Performance)
Conversational Spanish for the local (Elizabeth, NJ) customer base
responsibilities: Meet personal sales goals while motivating the team to drive overall store sales performance
Deliver and model exemplary customer service, maximizing profitability through the customer experience
Maintain store presentation — clean, well-organized, and compliant with visual-merchandising standards
Direct associates on the floor to ensure coverage and timely completion of daily tasks
Train and orient new associates to company standards and develop a sales-focused staff
Monitor associate performance, coach to company expectations, and recognize successes to build store morale
Serve as second-in-command, partnering with the Store Manager on day-to-day operational effectiveness

case.title: Acting ASM weekend: diagnose, staff, and coach Store #214 (Karl Lagerfeld Paris)
case.brief: You are the Assistant Sales Manager at Store #214, a Karl Lagerfeld Paris outlet under AM Retail Group. The Store Manager just left for a 4-day vacation and handed you the floor: the store is running behind plan and there is a new summer collection to set before Saturday's promo. Working only from the store's own operating documents (described below), produce the three artifacts an acting ASM would actually own this weekend — a read of where the sales gap really is, a Fri–Sun coverage plan, and a coaching/recognition plan — plus a short decisions log. The provided materials are a retail store's genuine operating documents (dashboards, KPI exports, a labor grid, a floor-set guide, the SM's handoff note) and fit this role directly, so no synthetic substitute is needed. Timebox is a hard 1.5 hours: we are testing judgment under real constraints, not exhaustiveness. Several of these documents are intentionally underspecified or quietly misleading — that mirrors a real Saturday when the SM is unreachable. Where the brief is silent, make a defensible call and record it; we care more about how you reason through the gaps than about a single 'right' answer.
case.repoSeed:
A shared drive for Store #214 (Karl Lagerfeld Paris, AM Retail Group), handed off while the Store Manager is on a 4-day vacation and you are acting ASM:
- `store_weekly_dashboard.xlsx` — last 4 weeks broken out by day: door traffic, transactions, conversion %, UPT, ADS, net sales, and sales-per-hour, each against plan. The current week closes ~8% under the net-sales plan; door traffic is down ~6% week-over-week, conversion has slipped from 22% to 19%, UPT is flat at 2.1, ADS is up slightly. The gap is genuinely mixed — there is no single clean cause.
- `associate_kpi_week.csv` — five associates: Dana (highest sales-per-hour in the store, but scheduled only Fri–Sat peak, conversion 15%, UPT 1.6 — a 'top performer' whose headline number is partly a scheduling artifact); Marek (keyholder, was the #1 seller last quarter, sales-per-hour down three weeks running, with a note that he's been covering extra opens since a co-worker quit); Lucie (keyholder, steady, conversion 24%, dependable); Petra (few hours but the highest UPT and ADS — strong at add-ons and clienteling); Tom (new hire, week 3, low across the board but trending up each week).
- `labor_schedule_grid.xlsx` + `labor_budget.txt` — the blank weekend grid and a hard 120-hour weekly labor cap; 88 hours are already committed Mon–Thu, leaving 32 hours for Fri–Sun.
- `floorset_guide_summer_drop.pdf` — the new summer-collection floor-set with a fixture map; the guide notes the set takes 2 people about 6 hours and must be complete before Saturday's promo opens.
- `sm_handoff_note.md` — the Store Manager's note: 'We're behind for the week — need you to bring it home this weekend. Set the summer drop, keep the floor covered, and don't blow labor. Call me only if it's on fire.'
- `service_incidents_log.md` — two clienteling notes, including a customer who waited at an unattended fitting room during Saturday peak and left without buying — the note does not say whether an associate neglected the customer or the floor was simply short at peak.
tasks: Diagnose the sales gap (≈½ page). Using `store_weekly_dashboard.xlsx` and `associate_kpi_week.csv`, state where the store is actually losing the ~8% it's behind plan — traffic, conversion, UPT, or ADS — and name the 2–3 highest-leverage moves genuinely within an ASM's control this weekend. Call out explicitly which portion of the gap you do NOT believe you can move this weekend, and why.

Build the Fri–Sun coverage plan. Fill in `labor_schedule_grid.xlsx` so the selling floor is covered through peak, the summer-drop floor-set in `floorset_guide_summer_drop.pdf` is complete before Saturday's promo, a keyholder (only Marek and Lucie hold keys) is on every open and every close, and you stay inside the 120-hour weekly cap from `labor_budget.txt` (32 hours remain for the weekend). If you cannot satisfy every constraint at once, show the trade-off you chose rather than quietly breaking one.

Write the coaching + recognition plan. For each of the five associates in `associate_kpi_week.csv`, give one concrete next action (coach / recognize / train / hold steady) tied to their actual numbers. Include the opening line you would really use with Marek and with Tom. Then reconcile the fitting-room walkout in `service_incidents_log.md`: decide whether it's an individual coaching moment or a coverage/process gap, and justify it from the data.

Keep a DECISIONS log (`DECISIONS.md`) as you go — normal practice when you're covering for the SM. For every call where the brief was open (the true size and cause of the gap, how you read Dana's sales-per-hour, how you sequenced the floor-set against peak coverage, how you handled the service incident), record in one line each: what you chose, the alternative you rejected, and the single question you'd put to the Store Manager when she's back.

coverProbes.where: `store_weekly_dashboard.xlsx` read against `sm_handoff_note.md` — the SM frames it as 'bring it home this weekend' (sell harder), but the data is a mixed traffic-and-conversion gap, not a pure selling gap.
coverProbes.reveals: Naive response accepts the goal at face value and prescribes generic 'push the team harder' energy. A good response decomposes the gap — separating traffic (largely outside ASM control this weekend) from conversion / UPT / ADS (coachable on-floor levers) — commits to the single highest-leverage lever for the timeframe, and is honest that part of the gap is traffic-driven and not recoverable by Sunday.
decisionSpace: Treat it primarily as a conversion problem and drive on-floor selling behaviors (greeting, fitting-room engagement) — fastest lever, but over-coaches a fundamentally fine team if traffic is the real driver.
Treat it as a UPT/ADS problem and push attach/add-on selling and clienteling (Petra's strength) — higher-margin and durable, but slower to move the weekend number.

Flag the goal as traffic-constrained, protect team morale, and surface it to the SM rather than chase an unreachable number — honest and fair, but risks reading as 'making excuses' instead of owning the floor.

coverProbes.where: `labor_schedule_grid.xlsx`, `labor_budget.txt`, and `floorset_guide_summer_drop.pdf` together — coverage, keyholder presence, the 6-hour two-person floor-set, and the 32 remaining hours cannot all be maximized at once.
coverProbes.reveals: A one-shot schedule that merely 'looks covered' will typically bust the 120-hour cap, schedule the floor-set during peak selling (pulling two people off the floor and tanking conversion), or leave an open/close with no keyholder (Marek/Lucie are the only two). A good response checks the plan against all three constraints explicitly and names which trade-off it accepted instead of silently violating one.
decisionSpace: Set the floor-set off-peak (Thursday close / Friday open) with two associates and accept a slightly thinner Friday-open floor — protects peak selling and stays on budget.
Authorize limited overtime to set the drop without pulling peak coverage — protects both the floor and the set, but breaches the labor cap and hurts sales-per-hour, so it really needs SM sign-off.
Phase the set — stand up the promo fixtures for Saturday and finish the rest Sunday/Monday — stays on budget and covered, but the store isn't fully to visual standard for the weekend.

coverProbes.where: `associate_kpi_week.csv` — Dana's headline sales-per-hour and Marek's three-week decline both look obvious until you read the scheduling pattern and the co-worker-quit note buried in the data.
coverProbes.reveals: Naive response rewards Dana's per-hour number, holds her up as the model, and writes Marek up as a performance problem. A good response recognizes Dana's number is inflated by peak-only scheduling (her 15% conversion means she's letting walk-by traffic leave) and reads Marek's dip as a probable workload/burnout signal from covering extra opens — something to investigate and support before judging.
decisionSpace: Reward Dana's sales-per-hour and give her more hours / hold her up as the example — ignores that her number is a peak-scheduling artifact and that her low conversion is leaving money on the floor.
Read the context: rebalance Dana's hours and coach her conversion/UPT, and treat Marek's decline as a likely workload issue to address with him before any performance framing.

Shift hours toward the all-around steady performers (Lucie/Petra) and coach Dana on the gap — improves overall store conversion, but risks de-motivating a high earner if the conversation is handled bluntly.

coverProbes.where: `service_incidents_log.md` — the unattended-fitting-room walkout doesn't state whether an associate neglected the customer or the floor was simply short-staffed at Saturday peak.
coverProbes.reveals: Naive response pins it on the nearest associate as a coaching write-up. A good response connects it to the weekend coverage gap (a staffing/zone-ownership root cause) versus an individual behavior, and only coaches a specific person if the schedule and zoning data actually support that it was a personal lapse.
decisionSpace: Coach the associate on fitting-room / zone ownership — fast and reinforces standards, but unfair if the floor was genuinely uncovered at peak.

Treat it as a coverage/process gap and fix it structurally (zone assignments, a named fitting-room owner per shift) — addresses the likely root cause, but lets a real individual lapse slide if that's what it was.
Gather signal first — check who was zoned there and the traffic spike at that hour — before acting; most accurate, but slower and defers the fix the SM wants made now.
